strengths: Addresses a genuine clinical problem: existing deep learning CT methods are tied to fixed acquisition settings; this work enables generalization across sampling rates and resolutions without retraining

Principled technical design combining neural operators (DISCO) with domain-specific adaptations: rotation-equivariant convolutions in polar coordinates respect CT geometry; joint spatial-frequency sinogram learning is well-motivated by Fourier slice theorem and classical FBP

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple sampling rates (9, 18, 36, 72 views), datasets, and diverse baselines (classical methods, CNNs, transformers, diffusion models) with strong consistent improvements (4 dB over CNNs, 3 dB over diffusion with 500× speedup)
Solid ablation studies validating design choices (rotation equivariance provides 0.83 dB PSNR gain; frequency-domain learning variants show detector-axis FFT is optimal)
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, baseline specifications, and comprehensive supplementary material enable validation and reproduction
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of architecture and design justification; well-motivated progression from problem statement through technical solution
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core components (DISCO operators, neural operators for imaging, unrolled networks) are not new; contribution is primarily application of existing techniques to CT rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation

Incomplete evaluation scope constrains impact: (1) Only 2D slices evaluated; 3D extension stated as future work limits immediate clinical applicability; (2) Only two anatomical sites tested; (3) No clinical validation despite claims of clinical utility; (4) Purely computational metrics without radiologist assessment of diagnostic quality

Experimental fairness concerns: Diffusion baselines (DPS, ALD) evaluated on only 500 test slices due to computational cost (footnote p.7) while other methods use full test sets, making direct comparison questionable and potentially biasing results in favor of proposed method

Overstated claims requiring caveats: (1) 'Resolution-independent' conflates continuous function space learning with true infinite-resolution invariance; method still requires discretization at inference; (2) 'Zero-shot super-resolution' tested via upsampling intermediate reconstructions rather than rigorous SR protocol; (3) Rotation equivariance only handles SO(2) symmetry with validation limited to 3 discrete rotations—quantitative continuous rotation evaluation needed

Insufficient analysis of practical applicability: (1) No investigation of training data requirements or performance degradation with limited data; (2) Handling of metal artifacts, motion artifacts not discussed; (3) Limited-angle CT mentioned in related work but not evaluated; (4) Generalization beyond 2D parallel/fan-beam geometry not demonstrated

Missing theoretical rigor: (1) No convergence analysis or bounds on discretization error as resolution increases despite claims of discretization-agnostic learning; (2) No statistical significance testing between methods despite overlapping error bars in some results; (3) Sensitivity to hyperparameter choices (kernel radius, basis functions) not explored

Potential baseline issues: CNN baseline operates only in image-space while CTO uses sinogram-space operators; sinogram-space CNN baseline would clarify value of DISCO over standard convolutions; diffusion baseline subset evaluation compromises fair comparison

strengths: Addresses practically relevant problem of resolution/sampling-rate agnostic CT reconstruction with clear clinical motivation
Technically sound dual-domain design combining sinogram-space (polar coordinates, frequency learning) and image-space processing
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple sampling rates, datasets, and includes zero-shot super-resolution and ablation studies
Strong empirical results: 4dB PSNR gain over CNNs, 3dB over diffusion methods, 500× faster inference
Well-motivated design choices: sinogram frequency learning inspired by FBP, rotation handling through circular padding with theoretical justification
Excellent reproducibility: detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, architectural specifications provided; clear presentation
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: applies existing DISCO [23] and UDNO [22] frameworks to CT without introducing new architectural or theoretical contributions

Overstated generalization claims: all methods trained jointly on all four sampling rates (multi-task learning), not true cross-rate generalization; true generalization would require training on subset of rates and testing on unseen rates
Rotation equivariance claims are imprecise: circular padding provides θ-shift equivariance in sinogram space, not inherent rotation equivariance in image space; ablation shows modest 0.83dB gain

Narrow evaluation scope: only 2D slices (3D deferred to future work), two datasets, no cross-dataset evaluation, resolution tested only at 256-512 (2× variation), missing evaluation on limited-angle CT and extreme undersampling

Evaluation fairness concerns: diffusion models only evaluated on 500/10,000 slices; joint training on all rates means single-rate baselines not optimized; no inference speed comparison with other single-pass methods
Insufficient analysis of mechanism: limited ablations on why polar coordinates help, no analysis of learned features, missing justification for performance gains beyond empirical results
Missing critical experiments: no train-on-one-rate-test-on-another evaluation, no cross-dataset generalization, no noise robustness study, no failure case analysis
Reproducibility gaps: no code release mentioned, exact mechanism of combining NOs,spatial and NOs,freq outputs unclear, hyperparameter selection process not documented

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with theoretically principled solution using neural operators in function space
Technically sound architecture with proper rotation equivariance formulation and joint spatial-frequency domain learning inspired by classical FBP
Strong experimental results showing consistent 4dB PSNR improvement over CNNs and 500× speedup over diffusion across multiple sampling rates
Comprehensive ablation studies validating key design choices (e.g., 0.83dB gain from rotation equivariance)
Demonstrates true zero-shot capability for super-resolution without retraining in both image and sinogram domains
Clear presentation with detailed methodology, informative visualizations, and extensive supplementary material (61 pages)
weaknesses: Severely limited dataset diversity: only 2 anatomical regions (kidney and abdomen) from same imaging modality undermines generalization claims for clinical deployment
Absence of clinical validation: no radiologist evaluation or assessment of diagnostic utility despite claims about practical applicability
Incomplete diffusion comparison: baseline evaluated on only 500 slices (5% of test set) due to computational cost, making the 3dB advantage claim unverified on full test set
Architectural design choices insufficiently justified: no sensitivity analysis for number of cascades, basis functions, or radius cutoff; hyperparameter tuning process vague
Generalization claims need refinement: training uses all sampling rates equally, so not truly zero-shot for unseen rates; unclear how model performs on out-of-distribution acquisition settings
Computational efficiency incompletely characterized: inference time compared only to diffusion not to CNN baseline; memory requirements and training time not discussed
Missing theoretical analysis: no empirical validation of DISCO's discretization-agnostic convergence or error bounds; quadrature approximation error not analyzed
Reproducibility gaps: code availability not mentioned, exact DISCO parameterization and quadrature implementation not fully specified, hyperparameter tuning procedure vague
Limited to 2D: clinical adoption requires 3D performance; generalization from 2D to 3D polar coordinates unexplored
Modest incremental contribution: primarily applies existing neural operator framework to new domain rather than introducing fundamentally novel concepts

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing a genuine clinical limitation: methods overfit to fixed acquisition setups, failing to generalize across sampling rates—a critical issue in clinical practice where settings vary across organs and protocols

Principled domain-aware design with clever exploitation of CT geometry: rotation-equivariant DISCO via flipped circular padding (Eq. 15), frequency-domain sinogram processing justified by Fourier slice theorem, and natural extension from Cartesian to polar coordinates

Comprehensive experimental validation with multiple large-scale datasets (10,000 kidney slices, 5,936 AAPM slices, 1,018 LIDC images), diverse baselines (learning-free, diffusion, CNNs, transformers, unrolled networks), thorough ablations validating each design choice, and zero-shot super-resolution results

Strong empirical results: 3.4+ dB PSNR gains over CNN baseline across multiple sampling rates, 3 dB over state-of-the-art diffusion with 500× faster inference, and consistent improvements across 9-, 18-, 36-, 72-view settings demonstrating practical value

Excellent reproducibility: detailed implementation (Secs. 5.1, B), extensive supplementary material with additional results and OOD tests, Bayesian hyperparameter search methodology, and fair comparison protocol across all methods

Technical soundness with proper treatment of boundary conditions and principled use of DISCO discretization-convergence properties; unrolled network framework grounded in established optimization theory
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (DISCO [25,34], unrolled networks [2,3,11], U-Net [41]) applied to CT with domain-specific engineering; rotation-equivariance via circular padding, while effective, is relatively straightforward; main contribution is systems/application rather than methodological innovation

Narrow dataset scope: only 2 main CT datasets (AAPM, Kidney) in main results; LIDC-IDRI relegated to supplementary; all 2D slice-based rather than 3D volumetric; no real clinical data with authentic noise, metal artifacts, or motion; limited anatomical diversity (missing cardiac, interventional protocols)

Multi-rate training protocol conflates architectural benefits with training strategy: baseline methods designed for single-rate, perform differently than original papers; while 'equal data per rate' is reasonable, doesn't reflect actual deployment; harder to isolate whether gains stem from NO architecture or training scheme

Modest improvements in key OOD scenarios undermine generalization claims: cross-dataset transfer only 9.8 dB (single direction Kidney→AAPM), noisy sinogram robustness only 3.06 dB (much smaller than in-distribution 3-4 dB gains), rotation equivariance contributes only 0.83 dB (Table 5)—suggesting advantages narrower than headlines suggest

Absent clinical validation despite medical imaging focus: no radiologist studies, no diagnostic accuracy evaluation (lesion detection, clinical utility), no integration feasibility analysis; purely quantitative metrics without discussion of clinical acceptability or workflow integration

Limited theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees or error bounds for resolution-agnostic property; DISCO's discretization-convergence cited but not analyzed in CT context; why NOs fundamentally superior to multi-scale CNNs not rigorously explored; rotational equivariance theory (Eqs. 7-14) could be more rigorous

Incomplete architectural exploration: other NO variants (FNO, LocalNO) only in supplementary discussion without empirical validation; FNO dismissed on principle but not tested; zero-shot super-resolution limited to single resolution doubling (256→512) with upsampled ground truth rather than independent high-res data

Computational training overhead not adequately addressed: 42% more FLOPs during training vs. CNN (4.68 vs 3.28 MFLOPs at 256×256, Sec. D.2); while inference comparable after pre-computation, training time slower and under-discussed; no wall-clock comparisons

Experimental design fairness concerns: different training epochs for baselines (100 for DuDoTrans, 200 for RegFormer, 2000 for diffusion) potentially introduces bias; Bayesian hyperparameter search for DISCO not explicitly mentioned for baselines; CNN timing missing from Table 2b

Limited failure mode analysis: no discussion of challenging cases (extreme undersampling, metal artifacts, anatomical variants); no analysis of when CTO underperforms; artifact types and edge cases not explored; ground truth from simulation rather than clinical gold standards

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (AAPM, Kidney, LIDC-IDRI) with detailed ablation studies and supplementary analysis
Addresses a clinically relevant problem: single-model generalization across varying CT acquisition protocols reduces deployment burden
Strong empirical results with consistent improvements (3-4 dB PSNR over CNN baselines, 6 dB over DuDoTrans on AAPM 18-view)
Well-documented implementation details and reproducibility considerations; code availability promised
Clear presentation with effective visual illustrations of the approach (Figures 1-3 explaining DISCO and rotation equivariance)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is applying existing DISCO convolutions [25, 34] to CT in a standard dual-domain unrolled network architecture; dual-domain CT methods are already well-established in literature [28, 31, 49, 52, 61]

Experimental confounds: Table 2a reveals multi-rate training helps all baselines substantially; Table 8 shows ~40% of CTO's reported gain over CNN (2.43 dB) comes from training scheme, not DISCO itself; single-rate comparison gives only 1.59 dB advantage
Parameter mismatch: main results use CTO with 1.1× parameters relative to CNN baseline (Table 11), inflating apparent gains; matched-parameter comparison shows more modest 1.97 dB improvement

Weak theoretical justification: paper advocates infinite-dimensional function space learning but trains on discrete grids; practical advantage over standard convolutions not theoretically established; discretization-convergence property referenced but not analyzed for CT context

Overclaimed contributions: 'first neural operator for CT' (applying existing tech is incremental), 'resolution-agnostic' (requires joint multi-resolution training), 'rotation-equivariant' (reduces to circular padding with only 0.83 dB ablation gain—Table 5)

Diffusion baseline concerns: DPS achieves only 25.68 dB vs. CTO's 31.57 dB (AAPM 18-view), anomalously weak; unclear if equal hyperparameter tuning effort applied; affects validity of '500× faster' and '3dB gain' claims
Zero-shot super-resolution uses bilinearly interpolated ground truth (p. 13), not true high-resolution anatomy; results inflated and clinically unrealistic

Limited scope: 2D-only evaluation (no 3D volumetric reconstruction), no clinical reader studies or outcome validation, niche problem (multi-rate generalization not primary use case for most practitioners)

Missing neural operator comparisons: paper argues why FNO unsuitable for imaging (Section D.1) but provides no empirical comparisons with other NO architectures (DeepONet, LocalNO) in main results, weakening core claims

Large cross-dataset transfer gain (9.8 dB over CNN, Section C.5) suggests CNN overfitting rather than demonstrating DISCO superiority; insufficient evidence that this represents true domain generalization

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine clinical limitation of existing methods overfitting to fixed acquisition settings
Technically sound approach leveraging DISCO's proven discretization-convergence properties for resolution-agnosticism
Clever rotation-equivariant design via flipped circular padding that respects CT geometry and π-periodicity
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (AAPM, Kidney, LIDC-IDRI), sampling rates (9/18/36/72 views), and scenarios (zero-shot super-resolution, OOD generalization)
Strong empirical results: 3.4+ dB PSNR over CNN, 3 dB over diffusion with 500× speedup, consistent across datasets
Excellent presentation with clear writing, well-designed figures (especially Fig. 1 and 3), and thorough supplementary material
Fair experimental setup with multi-rate co-training for all baselines and extensive ablations validating each component (+0.83 dB rotational equivariance, -4.82 dB without NOₛ)
Detailed reproducibility information including hyperparameter search methodology (Bayesian optimization), baseline implementations, and complexity analysis
weaknesses: Limited fundamental algorithmic novelty: primarily applies existing DISCO convolutions and UDNO architectures to CT rather than developing new methods; rotation-equivariance via circular padding is relatively straightforward

Weak theoretical foundation: no formal analysis of why function-space learning improves generalization across resolutions; lacks approximation error bounds despite citing discretization-convergence; no convergence analysis of unrolled optimization (Eq. 4)

Architectural design choices incompletely justified: cascaded dual-domain design noted as 'necessary for SOTA' contradicts claim that main contribution is function-space formulation; dual sinogram branches (spatial + frequency) shown empirically to help (2.7 dB detector-axis FFT gain) but lack principled explanation

Experimental scope limitations: only 2D CT evaluated (3D performance unknown, critical for clinical practice); only parallel-beam and fan-beam geometries; small AAPM test set (526 slices) with wide confidence intervals; no clinical validation or deployment feasibility analysis

OOD generalization results modest: cross-dataset transfer yields only ~1 dB gain at 18-view despite multi-rate training claims; diffusion baselines evaluated on 500-image subset only, introducing sampling bias

Missing technical analysis: no quantitative robustness metrics under arbitrary rotations (Fig. 3c shows only 0°/90°/180°); training time not compared with baselines; DISCO quadrature error (Eq. 12) not empirically quantified
Important results relegated to supplement: 9-view AAPM (Table 7), OOD generalization (C.5), LIDC-IDRI (Table 9); code repository link missing (abstract shows 'available at .')

Limited discussion of practical deployment: when does resolution-agnosticism provide clinical benefit vs. scenario-specific training? How do multi-rate training dynamics affect single-rate performance? No analysis of failure modes or anatomically-specific performance degradation
